examples.ru: [Мы] с братом живём в одной комнате.
examples.en: My brother and I live in the same room.
Olga and I work together.

note:
The Russian «мы с + instrumental» means exactly two people: I and that person. It is the usual way to say 'Masha and I'.

• «Мы с Ма́шей идём в кино́» - Masha and I are going to the movies
• «Мы с бра́том» - my brother and I

The verb is plural: идём, not «иду». The pronoun мы stays even though English has only 'Masha and I'.

For more people: «Мы с Ма́шей и Ко́лей».
title: Мы с Ма́шей: 'Masha and I'

examples.en: I went to the movies with her.
I'm bored without him.

note:
The 3rd-person personal pronouns add the letter «н» after a preposition:

• он, оно́ → у него́, с ним, о нём
• она́ → у неё, с ней, к ней
• они́ → у них, с ни́ми, к ним

The possessives его́, её, их stay the same:
• «У него́ есть соба́ка. Э́то его́ соба́ка.»

An exception are prepositions that come from verbs, e.g. благодаря́: благодаря́ ему́ (no «н»).
title: «Н» after prepositions: у него́, у неё, у них

examples.ru: [С пе́рвым днём весны́]! Скоро будет тепло.
examples.en: Happy first day of spring! It will be warm soon.

note:
In the Russian reckoning the seasons begin on the first day of a month, not on the equinox or solstice:

• 1 декабря́ - зима́ (winter)
• 1 ма́рта - весна́ (spring)
• 1 ию́ня - ле́то (summer)
• 1 сентября́ - о́сень (autumn)

So people say «С пе́рвым днём весны́!» even when there is still snow on the ground.
title: The first day of spring: March 1

examples.ru: Не давай ему сесть себе на [ше́ю].
examples.en: Don't let him take advantage of you.

related.en: to take advantage of someone, to freeload off someone

note:
«Сесть на ше́ю» - literally 'to sit on someone's neck' - means to exploit someone's kindness or leniency and give nothing in return.

• Не дава́й ему́ сесть тебе́ на ше́ю. - Don't let him take advantage of you.
• Он сиди́т на ше́е у роди́телей. - He is living off his parents.

The full version: сесть на ше́ю и но́жки све́сить - 'to sit on someone's neck and dangle your legs'.
title: Сесть на ше́ю: to take advantage of someone

examples.ru: Он подарил ей [буке́т] из пяти роз.
examples.en: He gave her a bouquet of five roses.
The veterans were presented with red carnations.

note:
On a first date a Russian man usually brings flowers: a bouquet or a single ро́за.

Гвозди́ки (carnations) are a different story:
• they are taken to cemeteries and monuments
• on May 9 they are given to veterans

The number of flowers matters too: an odd number (three, five, seven) is for the living, an even number for a funeral or a commemoration. So twelve roses is not an ordinary gift.
title: Flowers in Russia: roses yes, carnations no

examples.ru: Первого сентября дети идут в школу с [цвета́ми].
examples.en: On September 1, children go to school with flowers.

note:
The first school day is September 1 and it is called День зна́ний (Knowledge Day).

• children bring flowers to their teachers
• speeches are given at the ceremony in the schoolyard (лине́йка)
• for first-graders, a girl with a bell sits on the shoulder of a graduating senior (выпускни́к) - hence the name Пе́рвый звоно́к (First Bell)

Teachers have their own holiday on October 5, День учи́теля: pupils and parents give them flowers and congratulate them.
title: Knowledge Day and Teachers' Day

examples.en: You did great today!
Guys, well done.

related.en: well done; a fine fellow, a hero

note:
Молоде́ц is pronounced «маладе́ц» (an unstressed «о» sounds like «а»).

It means 'well done, good job':
• Ты молоде́ц! - Well done!
• Вы молодцы́! - Good for you all!

It is said to a woman too: Ма́ша, ты молоде́ц! The form does not change, because молоде́ц is in fact a masculine noun (a fine young man, a hero).
title: Молоде́ц: pronunciation and meaning

examples.en: - Are you coming with us? - Nah, probably not.
No, no, everything is fine, don't worry.

note:
In conversation да often does not mean 'yes' but softens the answer.

• Да нет, не на́до. - Oh no, no need.
• Да нет, всё норма́льно. - No, no, everything is fine.
• Да нет, наве́рное. - I don't think so, probably not.

Да нет is a gentle 'no': the speaker hedges and may change their mind.

Conversely, Да ну! expresses disbelief: no way!
title: Да нет, наверное: a 'yes' that means 'no'

examples.ru: Кто не [риску́ет], тот не пьёт шампанского.
examples.en: He who doesn't take risks doesn't drink champagne.

note:
The English 'nothing ventured, nothing gained' has a festive taste in Russian:

• Кто не риску́ет, тот не пьёт шампа́нского.

The saying is used when someone hesitates before a decisive step.

Note the genitive шампа́нского after the negated verb «не пьёт». The accusative шампа́нское is also heard, but the saying usually has the genitive.
title: Кто не рискует, тот не пьёт шампанского

examples.en: The guests shouted 'Gorko!' ('Bitter!') and the newlyweds kissed.

note:
At a Russian wedding the guests shout «Го́рько!» ('Bitter!') and the newlyweds must kiss while the guests count the seconds aloud.

The usual explanation is that the drink is 'bitter' and a kiss 'sweetens' it.

• сва́дьба - wedding
• молодожёны - newlyweds
• тамада́ - toastmaster, leads the toasts and the games

A Russian wedding has more talking than dancing: every guest gives a toast.
title: Го́рько! at a Russian wedding

examples.ru: У двери подруги потребовали [вы́куп] с жениха.
examples.en: At the door the bride's friends demanded a ransom from the groom.

note:
The 'ransom of the bride' exists in Russia too, but as a game:
• the bride's friends wait for the жени́х at the door
• they ask questions and set tasks (where is the key, when was the first kiss)
• a wrong answer is paid for with money or sweets

Afterwards the couple go to the ЗА́ГС (the registry office); a church wedding usually comes only after the civil one.
title: The bride ransom: a game at the door

examples.en: The parents greeted the newlyweds with a wedding loaf.

note:
When the newlyweds arrive at the restaurant, the parents greet them with a карава́й: a large round loaf served with salt.

The couple bite off a piece at the same time. Whoever bites off more will, as the belief goes, be the head of the family.

Bread and salt is a traditional welcome for a guest in general: хлеб да соль.
title: Карава́й: bread for the newlyweds

examples.en: The children are watching a cartoon about Cheburashka.

note:
When Russians talk about their childhood, these cartoons often come up:
• «Ну, погоди́!» - a wolf chases a hare
• «Просто́квашино» - дя́дя Фёдор, the cat Матро́скин and the dog Ша́рик
• «Крокоди́л Ге́на и Чебура́шка»
• «Ви́нни-Пух» - the Soviet version of Winnie-the-Pooh

A cartoon is a мультфи́льм, colloquially a му́льтик.
title: Soviet cartoons every Russian knows

examples.en: On May 9 Russia marks Victory Day.

note:
Russians call the war on the Soviet front the Вели́кая Оте́чественная война́ (1941-1945).

• it began on June 22, 1941, when Germany attacked the USSR
• May 9 is День Побе́ды, the main day of remembrance
• ветера́ны are given flowers, often red carnations

The term does not mean the whole of World War II: for that there is Втора́я мирова́я война́.
title: The Great Patriotic War

examples.en: Don't whistle in the house, there won't be any money!

note:
Russians do not whistle indoors: a superstition says the money will leave the house.

• Не свисти́, а то де́нег не бу́дет! - Don't whistle, or you'll have no money!
• свисте́ть - to whistle

Similar household habits:
• не здоро́ваться че́рез поро́г - greeting across the threshold brings a quarrel
• присе́сть на доро́жку - before a trip everyone sits down for a moment in silence
title: Don't whistle or you'll lose your money

examples.ru: Потяни дверь на [себя́], а не от себя.
examples.en: Pull the door toward you, don't push it away.

note:
On doors in Russia you see:
• На себя́ - pull (toward you)
• От себя́ - push (away from you)

The verbs are тяну́ть (to pull) and толка́ть (to push). It is easy to get confused at a store entrance.

Потяни́ дверь на себя́, а не толка́й!
title: Pull and push: на себя́ and от себя́

examples.en: I know this city well.
She speaks Russian.

note:
Russian verbs have two sets of present-tense endings.

1st conjugation: зна́ть - зна́ю, зна́ешь, зна́ет, зна́ем, зна́ете, зна́ют
2nd conjugation: говори́ть - говорю́, говори́шь, говори́т, говори́м, говори́те, говоря́т

The 2nd conjugation includes verbs in -ить (except брить, стелить) and some in -еть and -ать: смотре́ть, ви́деть, слы́шать, держа́ть.

All the others (де́лать, чита́ть, рабо́тать) are 1st conjugation.
title: The present tense: 1st and 2nd conjugation

examples.en: I love hot tea.

examples.ru: Я каждый день [хожу́] на работу пешком.
examples.en: I walk to work every day.

related.en: to walk, to go on foot

note:
In some 2nd-conjugation verbs a consonant changes only in the 1st person singular:
• люби́ть: люблю́, лю́бишь (б - бл)
• ходи́ть: хожу́, хо́дишь (д - ж)
• плати́ть: плачу́, пла́тишь (т - ч)
• ви́деть: ви́жу, ви́дишь (д - ж)
• лови́ть: ловлю́, ло́вишь (в - вл)

The stress moves too: хожу́, but хо́дишь, хо́дят.
title: Consonant changes in the 1st person: люблю́, хожу́, плачу́

examples.en: A ladybug landed on my palm.

note:
A ladybug is бо́жья коро́вка in Russian, literally 'God's little cow'.

Children let it crawl onto the palm and sing to it to fly away to the sky:
• Бо́жья коро́вка, улети́ на не́бо! - Ladybug, fly away to the sky!

The rhyme has many variants.
title: Ladybug in Russian: бо́жья коро́вка

examples.ru: Мы купили билеты, а рейс отменили. Вот тебе, бабушка, и [Ю́рьев] день!
examples.en: We bought tickets and the flight was canceled. Well, how about that!

note:
Ю́рьев день is St George's Day. George is Гео́ргий, in everyday speech Ю́рий or Его́р.

A well-known saying comes from it:
• Вот тебе́, ба́бушка, и Ю́рьев день! - Well, how about that: an unexpected disappointment, ruined plans.

Origin: peasants used to be allowed to change their landlord only around St George's Day. When the ruler abolished that right, the saying stayed.

It is said with grumbling, often jokingly.
title: Юрьев день: St George's Day and a saying

examples.ru: В [Ве́рбное] воскресенье мы пошли в церковь с вербой.
examples.en: On Palm Sunday we went to church with willow branches.
Grandma put some pussy willows in a vase.

note:
Palm Sunday (the Sunday before Easter) is Ве́рбное воскресе́нье in Russian.

In Russia the day is tied to the willow, not to palms or flowers:
• ве́рба - willow, its twigs are taken to church
• ве́рбочки - pussy willows
• Ла́зарева суббо́та - Lazarus Saturday, the day before

After Ве́рбное воскресе́нье comes Страстна́я неде́ля, Holy Week, the last week of Lent.
title: Palm Sunday in Russian: Вербное воскресенье

examples.en: He doesn't have a penny.
Will you pay cash or by card?

examples.ru: Родители дают мне [карма́нные] деньги раз в неделю.
examples.en: My parents give me pocket money once a week.

related.en: kopeck, a hundredth of a ruble

note:
A копе́йка is a hundredth of a ruble, and it lives on in sayings:
• у меня́ нет ни копе́йки - I don't have a penny
• ни гроша́ за душо́й - the same, a bit old-fashioned
• быть на ме́ли - to be broke

Other words:
• нали́чные - cash: плати́ть нали́чными
• ме́лочь - small change
• карма́нные де́ньги - pocket money

Де́ньги exists only in the plural: у меня́ мно́го де́нег.
title: Money: ни копейки, наличные, мелочь

examples.en: Our doctor said that everything is fine.
The school principal came to the lesson.

note:
Most Russian occupations are masculine nouns that are used for women too:
• она́ врач, она́ дире́ктор, она́ до́ктор, она́ инжене́р
• the verb agrees with the real sex: врач сказа́ла, дире́ктор пришла́

Some have a feminine form: учи́тельница, певи́ца, актри́са, писа́тельница, поэте́сса.

Forms in -ша (до́кторша) are colloquial and often jokey. Newer forms in -ка (а́вторка, блогерка) are rejected by many.

To stress the sex: же́нщина-врач.
title: Occupations and women: врач and дире́ктор have no feminine form

examples.ru: На празднике девушки водили [хорово́д] на поляне.
examples.en: On holidays the girls danced a round dance in the meadow.
Grandma put on a sarafan and a headscarf.

related.en: bast shoes, peasant footwear woven from bark

note:
Some words for the old Russian folk life:

• хорово́д - a circle dance with singing; води́ть хорово́д - to dance in a ring
• сарафа́н - a long sleeveless dress, the old women's folk costume
• руба́ха - a long folk shirt
• ла́пти - peasant shoes woven from bast (tree bark), not made of leather
title: Хорово́д, сарафа́н and ла́пти: folk dance and dress

examples.ru: В [роди́тельскую] субботу мы поехали на кладбище.
examples.en: On Memorial Saturday we went to the cemetery.
After the funeral there was a wake at a cafe.

note:
The days of remembering the dead are called роди́тельская суббо́та or помина́ние поко́йных.

• роди́тельская суббо́та - a Saturday when the dead are remembered and cemeteries are visited
• Дми́триевская суббо́та - the Saturday before November 8, St Demetrius' Day
• поми́нки - the memorial meal after a funeral

Flowers are usually taken to the grave.
title: Memorial Saturdays: роди́тельская суббо́та

examples.en: Put the pencil in the pencil case.
Old toys are lying in the chest.

note:
Russian has words of Turkic origin, some of them in very ordinary vocabulary:
• де́ньги - money
• каранда́ш - pencil, literally 'black stone'
• сунду́к - chest, trunk
• база́р - market; colloquially also an uproar: что за база́р?
title: Turkic loanwords in Russian: деньги, карандаш, сундук

examples.en: Christ is born! - We glorify Him!
Merry Christmas to you!

note:
The traditional Christmas greeting and its reply:
• Христо́с рожда́ется! - Сла́вите Его́! (Christ is born! - Glorify Him!)
• or Христо́с роди́лся! - Сла́вим Его́! (Christ has been born! - We glorify Him!)

The reply is 'Glorify Him' or 'We glorify Him', not 'Truly He is born'.

The usual short greeting is «С Рождество́м!», with «с» and the instrumental.
title: The Christmas greeting in Russian

examples.en: For dinner Mom made stuffed cabbage rolls.
Sour cream was served with the cabbage rolls.

note:
• голубцы́ - cabbage leaves stuffed with meat and rice, cooked in a sauce
• долма́ - stuffed grape leaves, from Caucasian cuisine

Голубцы́ have nothing to do with го́лубь, a pigeon: the dish is made of cabbage.

Голубцы́ are usually served with смета́на (sour cream).
title: Stuffed cabbage rolls: голубцы́

examples.ru: В зоопарке мы видели [слони́ху] с детёнышем.
examples.en: At the zoo we saw a female elephant with her calf.
Our cat had kittens.

note:
Russian often has a separate word for the female, formed with the suffixes -иц(а) and -их(а).

• лев - льви́ца, волк - волчи́ца
• медве́дь - медве́дица
• слон - слони́ха, ёж - ежи́ха

Some species have one name for both: ко́шка is a cat in general, while ко́т is specifically a tomcat. Лиса́ is a fox of either sex; the male ли́с is rarely heard.
title: Female animals: львица, волчица, слониха

examples.en: Our dog barks at every passer-by.
All night a horse neighed outside the window.

related.en: to neigh; colloquial: to laugh loudly

note:
People hear the same sounds differently in different languages, so the imitations differ.

• соба́ка - «гав-гав» (English 'woof')
• у́тка - «кря-кря» (English 'quack')
• свинья́ - «хрю-хрю» (English 'oink')
• ло́шадь - «иго-го» (English 'neigh')
• коро́ва - «му-у», пету́х - «ку-ка-ре-ку»

Verbs come from them: соба́ка ла́ет, у́тка кря́кает, свинья́ хрю́кает, коро́ва мычи́т, ло́шадь ржёт. Ржать is also colloquial 'to laugh loudly'.
title: How animals 'talk' in Russian

examples.en: This is a really cool movie.
Are you kidding me? I'm serious!

related.en: joke, prank; something funny or odd

note:
Прико́л and прико́льный belong to everyday, mostly younger speech.

• прико́л - a joke, something funny or unusual
• прико́льный - cool, fun, interesting
• прика́лываться - to joke around, to kid someone

«Ты что, прика́лываешься?» means 'Are you kidding me?'.

Прико́л в том, что... means 'the funny thing is that...'.

It sounds informal: fine among friends, not in an official conversation.
title: Прико́л and прика́лываться: colloquial slang

examples.en: Crap, I forgot my keys at home!
Mom made pancakes with jam.

note:
Блин is first of all a thin pancake.

But in conversation it is also an exclamation, a mild stand-in for a rude curse. People say it when something surprises, disappoints or annoys them:

• Блин, я опозда́л! - Crap, I'm late!
• Блин, как здесь краси́во! - Wow, it's beautiful here!

It is informal but not vulgar. Better not to say it to an older person or to your boss.
title: Блин: a pancake and an exclamation

examples.en: It seems to me that it's cold outside.
I think he needs a rest.

note:
Five common ways to say what you think:

• Я ду́маю, что... - I think that...
• Я счита́ю, что... - I consider that...
• Мне ка́жется, что... - It seems to me that...
• На мой взгляд... - In my view...
• «С мое́й то́чки зре́ния...» - From my point of view...

The clause always starts with что ('that'), preceded by a comma: Я ду́маю, что он прав. English can drop 'that', Russian cannot.

Note: по-мо́ему is written with a hyphen and means 'in my opinion'.
title: How to give your opinion in Russian

examples.en: Please bring the check.
I wish you happiness and health!

note:
When «с» and «ч» stand next to each other in a Russian word, they are pronounced together as a long soft «щ».

• счёт - read as «щёт», bill
• сча́стье - «ща́стье», happiness
• счита́ть - «щита́ть», to count
• расчёска - «ращёска», comb
• чересчу́р - «чирищу́р», too much

The same goes for зч and жч: зака́зчик (customer) is read as «зака́щик».

The spelling does not show it: it is written «с» + «ч».
title: Reading сч as щ

examples.en: I wish you success in your studies!

examples.ru: Мы [пригласи́ли] всех друзей на Новый год.
examples.en: We invited all our friends to celebrate New Year with us.
Grandma gave me a warm scarf.

note:
Verbs of greeting and gifts have their own patterns.

• жела́ть кому́ чего́ - to wish someone something (the thing wished for is in the genitive): жела́ю вам здоро́вья
• дари́ть кому́ что - to give someone something as a present: дари́ть цветы́
• приглаша́ть кого́ куда́ - to invite someone somewhere: в го́сти
• украша́ть, наряжа́ть что - to decorate: наряжа́ть ёлку

Perfectives: пожела́ть, подари́ть, пригласи́ть, укра́сить, наряди́ть.
title: Желать, дарить, приглашать: verbs of holidays

examples.en: We always see in the New Year at home.
Where did you celebrate last New Year?

note:
«Как Но́вый год встре́тишь, так его́ и проведёшь» - the way you welcome the New Year is how you will spend it.

So before the holiday Russians:
• finish important work and pay back debts
• forgive offenses
• buy new festive clothes

The verb встреча́ть means 'to meet', and with a holiday also 'to see in, to welcome': встреча́ть Но́вый год.
title: Seeing in the New Year: a Russian saying

examples.en: Olivier salad is always on the festive table.

examples.ru: К Новому году мы купили килограмм [мандари́нов].
examples.en: For New Year we bought a kilo of tangerines.

note:
New Year is the main family feast in Russia, and the dishes are almost always the same.

• оливье́ - Olivier salad, diced potatoes, vegetables and meat in mayonnaise
• селёдка под шу́бой - a layered salad of herring, potatoes, beets and carrots, literally 'herring under a fur coat'
• бутербро́ды с кра́сной икро́й - sandwiches with red caviar
• мандари́ны и шампа́нское - tangerines and champagne

Икра́ is fish roe: кра́сная икра́ is salmon roe, чёрная икра́ is black caviar.
title: The New Year table: оливье and селёдка под шубой

examples.ru: В [соче́льник] многие постятся до первой звезды.
examples.en: On Christmas Eve many people fast until the first star.
Children go from house to house singing carols.

note:
The day before Christmas is the соче́льник, and Christmas (January 7) is Рождество́.

• соче́льник - January 6; by custom nothing is eaten until the first star
• коля́дки - going from house to house singing, for sweets or money
• гада́ние - fortune-telling, especially during Свя́тки (January 7-19)
• Креще́ние - Epiphany, January 19
title: Сочельник and колядки: the Russian Christmas Eve

examples.en: She got a valentine from a secret admirer.

examples.ru: [Рома́шка] - символ Дня семьи, любви и верности.
examples.en: The daisy is the symbol of the Day of Family, Love and Fidelity.

related.en: Day of Family, Love and Fidelity

note:
February 14 is День влюблённых (День свято́го Валенти́на) in Russia too, but it is celebrated more modestly.

• валенти́нка - a heart-shaped card
• рома́шка - a daisy, the symbol of the other holiday

The official holiday is July 8: День семьи́, любви́ и ве́рности. It is tied to the saints Пётр and Февро́ния from the city of Му́ром, patrons of marriage.
title: Valentine's Day and the Day of Family in Russia

examples.ru: На Ма́сленицу мы печём [блины́] всю неделю.
examples.en: During Maslenitsa we bake pancakes all week.
Maslenitsa is celebrated before Great Lent.

note:
Ма́сленица is the week before Great Lent, and its main food is блины́. The name comes from ма́сло (butter).

The days have names:
1. Встре́ча - meeting
2. Заигры́ш - the start of the games
3. Ла́комка - the mother-in-law treats her son-in-law
4. Разгуля́й - revelry, jumping over the fire
5. Тёщины вечёрки - the son-in-law treats his mother-in-law
6. Золо́вкины посиде́лки - the young wife treats her husband's sister
7. Прово́ды - the farewell, Прощёное воскресе́нье

The holiday ends with the burning of a straw effigy.
title: Масленица: pancake week

examples.en: Enough partying - the good times don't last forever.

related.en: Maslenitsa, the week of merrymaking before Lent

note:
«Не всё ко́ту ма́сленица» - literally 'it's not always Maslenitsa for the cat': after the fun comes a time of restrictions.

The full saying continues: «..., бу́дет и вели́кий пост» - 'there will be Great Lent too'. Usually only the first part is said.

It is used when someone thinks the good days will last forever, much like 'the good times can't last forever'.
title: Не всё коту масленица: a saying

examples.en: Forgive me for being late.
God will forgive, and I forgive.

note:
The last Sunday of Maslenitsa is Прощёное воскресе́нье - Forgiveness Sunday. By custom people ask everyone for forgiveness.

1. You say: «Прости́ меня́!» - Forgive me!
2. The reply: «Бог прости́т, и я проща́ю» - God will forgive, and I forgive.
3. Or briefly: «И ты меня́ прости́» - And you forgive me too.

Прости́ is the imperative of прости́ть. The everyday 'sorry' is извини́ or прости́, but on that Sunday the phrase sounds more solemn.
title: Прощёное воскресенье: Forgive me

examples.en: We will win if we act together.
I will try to persuade him to stay.

note:
Some verbs have no 1st person singular (in the present tense, or in the future for perfectives) because it would sound unnatural.

• победи́ть - ты победи́шь, он победи́т, мы победи́м
• убеди́ть - ты убеди́шь, он убеди́т
• очути́ться - ты очути́шься, он очути́тся

The other forms are normal. For 'I' a workaround is used:
• я смогу́ победи́ть, я хочу́ победи́ть
• я постара́юсь убеди́ть
title: Verbs with no 'I' form: победить, убедить

examples.en: He seems to have already gone home.
Don't worry, everything is already done, after all.
He is unlikely to come today.

note:
Three particles that are hard to translate.

• вро́де - 'like' (вро́де тебя́ = someone like you) or 'it seems, apparently'
• ведь - 'after all', 'you know', 'because': it reminds the listener of what they already know, and is often left untranslated
• вряд ли - 'unlikely', 'hardly': strong doubt

Note: after вряд ли the sentence stays affirmative, with no «не»: Вряд ли он придёт - he is unlikely to come.
title: Вроде, ведь, вряд ли: three small words

examples.en: She speaks Russian well.
He has been studying the Russian language for five years.

note:
English 'speak Russian' takes a direct object, but the Russian verb of speaking does not.

• знать, изуча́ть, преподава́ть + ру́сский язы́к: я зна́ю ру́сский язы́к - I know Russian
• говори́ть, чита́ть, писа́ть, понима́ть + по-ру́сски or на ру́сском: я говорю́ по-ру́сски

Not: «я говорю́ ру́сский язы́к».

The same goes for other languages: по-англи́йски, по-неме́цки, по-францу́зски.
title: Русский язык or по-русски

examples.en: He is already forty years old.
The ticket costs fifty rubles.

note:
Among the tens only со́рок is unlike the others: it has nothing to do with четы́ре (four), as English 'forty' has with 'four'. One explanation: it was once a measure of 40 sable skins, enough for one fur coat.

Stress of the tens (often got wrong):
• де́сять, два́дцать, три́дцать, со́рок
• пятьдеся́т, шестьдеся́т - stressed on the ending
• се́мьдесят, во́семьдесят - stressed at the beginning
• девяно́сто
title: Сорок: the odd number 40 and the stress of the tens

examples.en: I need to make an appointment with a doctor.
Put on shoe covers before you go in.

note:
A поликли́ника is an outpatient clinic, where a Russian goes with an ordinary illness. Useful words:

• регистрату́ра - the front desk where you book an appointment
• записа́ться к врачу́ - to make an appointment with a doctor
• бахи́лы - disposable shoe covers
• гардеро́б - the coat check
• больни́чный - sick leave: я на больни́чном
• переры́в - a break: обе́денный переры́в

Note that гардеро́б is the coat check, while clothes in general are оде́жда.
title: At the doctor's in Russia: поликлиника, бахилы, регистратура

examples.ru: Он подарил маме [тюльпа́ны] на Восьмое марта.
examples.en: He gave his mom tulips for March 8.
Happy March 8!

note:
March 8 is a holiday and a day off in Russia. All women are congratulated: mothers, colleagues, friends, grandmothers.

• flowers, most often тюльпа́ны, and small gifts are given
• the working day before the holiday is shorter

Greeting: «Поздравля́ю тебя́ с Восьмы́м ма́рта!»

The date in a greeting is said 'with the eighth of March': the ordinal in the instrumental, the month in the genitive.
title: March 8 in Russia: Международный женский день

examples.en: Already washed up? Hope you enjoyed your steam bath!

note:
«С лёгким па́ром!» is said to someone who has just come out of a banya, a bath or a shower; literally 'with light steam'. The English counterpart is something like 'Hope you enjoyed it!'.

It is also the title of the favorite New Year movie «Иро́ния судьбы́, или С лёгким па́ром!» ('The Irony of Fate', 1976), which is shown on TV every year before New Year.
title: «С лёгким паром!»: a wish after a bath

examples.en: We are renting an apartment in the center.
Take off your jacket, it's hot in here.
He shot a new movie.

related.en: to film; to take off; to rent as a tenant
pf.: to film, to take off, to rent

note:
Снима́ть has several senses, and English needs different verbs for them:
• снима́ть фильм - to shoot a movie
• снима́ть пальто́ - to take off a coat
• снима́ть кварти́ру - to rent an apartment (as a tenant)
• снять де́ньги со счёта - to withdraw money from an account

The perfective is снять: сниму́, сни́мешь; снял, сняла́. The owner сдаёт an apartment, and the tenant снима́ет it.
title: Снимать: not only 'to shoot'

examples.en: Imagine, they transferred us to another office!
Imagine, we won tickets to Paris!

note:
Прики́нь (plural or polite прики́ньте) is slang for 'just imagine', said before a surprising piece of news. It is how friends talk; in a neutral tone say предста́вь(те).

The same verb in its standard meaning is 'to estimate roughly': прики́нуть расхо́ды - to work out the costs roughly.
title: Прикинь: 'imagine' in conversation

examples.en: - Shall we meet at seven? - Deal!
Green really suits you.
- Sorry, I forgot to call. - It's okay, forget it.

examples.ru: Наконец до меня [дошло́], в чём шутка.
examples.en: I finally got the joke.

note:
Russian motion verbs have figurative meanings too:
• Идёт! - Deal!
• Тебе́ идёт - it suits you (the person it suits is in the dative)
• Прое́хали - let's forget it (colloquial)
• До меня́ дошло́ - I got it, it dawned on me (colloquial)
title: Идти, проехать, дойти: motion verbs in figurative senses

examples.ru: Спроси Ивана, он на таких задачах собаку [съел].
examples.en: Ask Ivan, he is an old hand at problems like this.
She is an old hand at sales.

note:
The idiom has nothing to do with dogs: на чём-то соба́ку съесть means to be a real expert at something after long practice.

The closest English is 'to know something inside out' or 'to be an old hand at something'.

It is said about someone else or about yourself: Я на э́том соба́ку съел - I'm an old hand at it.
title: Собаку съесть: to be an expert at something

examples.en: Today everything is topsy-turvy for us.
He grabbed the boy by the scruff of the neck.

related.en: scruff, the back of the collar; the nape (colloquial)
inside out, the wrong way round

note:
Шиворот-навыворот means 'topsy-turvy, the wrong way round': де́лать всё ши́ворот-навы́ворот - to do everything wrong.

The first word is ши́ворот, colloquially the back of the collar or the nape of the neck: схвати́ть за ши́ворот - to grab by the scruff of the neck.
title: Шиворот-навыворот: topsy-turvy

examples.ru: Привезти ему яблоки из сада - [в Ту́лу] со своим самоваром.
examples.en: Bringing him apples from the garden is like carrying coals to Newcastle.

examples.ru: Дарить цветы флористу - всё равно что ехать [в Ту́лу] со своим самоваром.
examples.en: Giving flowers to a florist is like carrying coals to Newcastle.

related.en: samovar, a vessel for boiling water for tea
Tula, a city famous for its samovars

note:
Since the 18th century Tula has been known as the city of samovars. The idiom е́хать в Ту́лу со свои́м самова́ром means to bring something to a place where there is plenty of it.

The English equivalent is 'carrying coals to Newcastle'.

It is said when someone's effort or gift is pointless.
title: «В Ту́лу со свои́м самова́ром»: carrying coals to Newcastle

examples.en: I don't give a damn what they say about me.

examples.ru: Ему по [бараба́ну], что о нём думают.
examples.en: He doesn't care what people think of him.
I couldn't care less about your grudges.

note:
Russian has many colloquial ways to say 'I couldn't care less'. The indifferent person is in the dative.

• мне фиоле́тово - literally 'it's purple to me'
• мне по бараба́ну - 'it's on the drum to me'
• мне до ла́мпочки - 'it's up to the light bulb to me'
• мне наплева́ть - 'I spit on it'
• мне паралле́льно - 'it's parallel to me'

The neutral ones are мне всё равно́ or мне без ра́зницы - it makes no difference to me.

The colloquial forms are not for your boss or for formal talk.
title: I couldn't care less: мне фиоле́тово and other sayings

examples.en: But we agreed to meet at five.
But it's obvious!

related.en: emphasizing particle: but, after all, you know

note:
The particle же strengthens the word before it. English usually shows it with intonation or with words like 'but', 'after all', 'you know'.

• Ты же обеща́л! - But you promised!
• Ка́кая же ты у́мница! - How smart you are!
• Что же ты молчи́шь? - Well, why are you silent?

It stands after the word it stresses, never at the beginning of a sentence. Without же the same sentence sounds calmer.
title: The particle же: emphasis that is hard to translate

examples.ru: Он [завари́л] такую кашу, что все разбираются до сих пор.
examples.en: He made such a mess that everyone is still sorting it out.
In spring the roads are slush underfoot.

related.en: to brew, to pour boiling water over; завари́ть ка́шу - to stir up trouble
to face the consequences: расхлёбывать ка́шу

note:
Ка́ша (porridge) is also an image for a mess in Russian.

• завари́ть ка́шу - to stir up trouble
• расхлёбывать ка́шу - to face the consequences
• ка́ша под нога́ми - slush on the road
• ка́ша во рту́ - mumbled speech

A weak person is told: «Ты что, ка́ши ма́ло е́л?» - didn't you eat enough porridge?

Proverb: «Ка́шу ма́слом не испо́ртишь» - you can't spoil porridge with butter; a good thing can't be too good.
title: Каша in sayings: not only a dish

examples.en: He rode without a ticket the whole way.
On the bus I paid the fare by card.

related.en: hare; figuratively a passenger without a ticket

note:
A passenger without a ticket is called a за́яц ('hare'): е́хать за́йцем means to ride without paying.

• безбиле́тник - a fare dodger (the official word)
• контролёр - ticket inspector
• штраф - fine

The fare is called прое́зд: оплати́ть прое́зд. On a bus you will hear: «Оплати́те прое́зд, пожа́луйста» - Please pay the fare.
title: Riding without a ticket: ехать зайцем

examples.en: Happy upcoming New Year to you!
We wish you health and happiness!

note:
Russians congratulate in two ways:

• in the days before the holiday: «С наступа́ющим!» (short for «С наступа́ющим Но́вым го́дом!») - Happy upcoming New Year!
• after midnight: «С Но́вым го́дом!» - Happy New Year!

The verb жела́ть takes the genitive: жела́ю тебе́ сча́стья, здоро́вья, успе́ха.

The person is in the dative (тебе́), and what you wish is in the genitive (сча́стья).
title: New Year greetings: с наступающим and с Новым годом
